The giant armadillo  is the largest extant member of the order Cingulata, yet surprisingly little is known about its detailed life-history under controlled conditions. In a recent respirometry study, the resting metabolic rate of a captive adult female was determined to be 3028 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 3028 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at a core body temperature of 33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C], a standard thermal condition for the species during periods of inactivity. This basal oxygen consumption value, which reflects the high energetic cost of maintaining such a large body mass, is among the highest recorded for any xenarthran and aligns closely with allometric predictions for a mammal of 45 kilograms. The same individual, after parturition, provided data on neonatal mass; the newborn offspring weighed exactly 62.15 grams [Wwb = 62.15 grams], a relatively modest size for a mammal that eventually reaches a substantial adult body weight. This initial mass, recorded during the first day after birth, suggests that the altricial neonate is heavily dependent on maternal investment during the early phases of its development.

Gestation length in the species has been documented from a small number of captive breeding events. Under thermoneutral conditions approximating 33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C], the period from conception to parturition lasted 122 days [tg = 122 days], a duration that is comparatively protracted for a mammal of this size. This extended gestation likely reflects the considerable energetic investment required to produce a single, well-developed offspring. Following live birth, the neonatal individual enters a phase of intense dependency, with milk ingestion beginning immediately after teat attachment. The lactation period, or time spent as a suckling juvenile, continues until weaning occurs at 35 days after birth [tx = 35 days after birth] when maintained at a stable temperature of 33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C]. The weaning process itself involves a dietary transition from maternal milk to solid food, a critical milestone that marks the onset of nutritional independence for the growing juvenile.

Sexual maturation in Priodontes maximus is a comparatively slow process. Under the thermal regime typical of the species' active metabolic period (33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C]), the time from birth to the attainment of puberty has been estimated at 320 days [tp = 320 days]. This relatively late onset of gonadal maturation, when compared to other xenarthrans of similar body size, suggests that individuals invest heavily in somatic growth before diverting resources toward reproductive effort. The juvenile and sub-adult stages are thus characterized by a prolonged phase of mass gain and behavioral development. Interestingly, the maximum lifespan recorded under captive conditions has been documented at 5475 days [am = 5475 days] when maintained at 33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C]. This extended longevity aligns well with the predictions of a slow life-history strategy, where delayed reproduction is often coupled with an increased probability of survival into older age classes.

Reproductive output in this species is extremely low, consistent with its position as a large-bodied, slow-living mammal. Field and captive records indicate that females typically produce a single litter per year, with each litter containing on average 1.5 young [N_R_i = each litter containing on average 1.5 young]. The annual reproductive frequency, therefore, is one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year]. This combined annual output of approximately 1.5 offspring per year, when placed in the context of the species' maximum lifespan of roughly 5475 days, underscores a life-history strategy geared toward high parental investment per offspring rather than high fecundity. The ultimate wet weight attained by adults is considerable, with the heaviest individuals reaching a mass of approximately 45190 grams [Wwi = approximately 45190 grams]. This remarkable adult body mass, which can exceed 45 kilograms, places the giant armadillo well beyond the size range of all other armadillo species and carries profound implications for its feeding ecology, home range size, and metabolic demands.

The giant armadillo exemplifies an extreme life-history strategy, with each reproductive event requiring a substantial energy investment that constrains the population's resilience to environmental change. The low reproductive rate, characterized by a single offspring per litter and a maximum of one litter per year, reflects a strategy where parental investment is prioritized over fecundity. This is further supported by the extended period of dependency, from a 122-day gestation through a 35-day nursing period, ensuring that each offspring receives considerable maternal resources before facing independence. The combination of a relatively late age at puberty—estimated at 320 days after birth—and a maximum lifespan approaching 15 years aligns with theoretical predictions for a K-selected mammal. These traits, together with its highly specialized myrmecophagous diet, make the species particularly vulnerable to habitat fragmentation and hunting pressure, as low reproductive rates limit its capacity for population recovery.
